segments.english: Abraham was old and advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.
segments.literal: and-Abraham old came in-days; and-LORD blessed ACC-Abraham in-all

tokens.note: verb 'be old', perfect (qatal), 3rd masculine singular; it opens the background clause
idiom: 'come in the days' = be advanced in years
idiom: the plural 'days' with ב; 'in days' = advanced in years
the divine name; the pointing differs between witnesses (see apparatus)
piel perfect, God as subject: 'bless' (Pi 2); the perfect after the subject is background
בַּכֹּל: ב 'in' with כֹּל 'all'; the English adds 'things' for the idiom 'in all'

phrases.english: Abraham was old and advanced in years,
and the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.

grammar: The clause וְאַבְרָהָם זָקֵן בָּא בַּיָּמִים has a noun subject and a qatal, so it is background to the main clause, which is the blessing.
The idiom בָּא בַּיָּמִים, 'come in the days', means advanced in years; the English keeps it as one phrase and gives no age.
וַיהוָה בֵּרַךְ אֶת־אַבְרָהָם repeats the background pattern with the divine name as subject; 'had blessed' is that pluperfect.
The verse ends with בַּכֹּל, 'in all' (כֹּל with the article and ב); what the blessing consisted of is Ibn Ezra's gloss and stays in the commentary.
segments.note: The English gives the words only. What the blessing consisted of (length of days, wealth, honour, sons) is Ibn Ezra's gloss and is kept in the commentary. Rashi's numerical reading of בַּכֹּל is a midrash and is recorded, not followed.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: 'blessed in all' means in length of days, wealth, honour and sons, which he calls all of man's desire. He adds that the midrash which makes 'Bakkol' the name of a daughter of Abraham would have to add a further ב, a beth of service ('with Bakkol'), which the text lacks. The English 'in all things' takes the preposition and the word as they stand; his list of what the blessing was stays in the note.
Rashi: בַּכֹּל has the numerical value of בֵּן (son, 52), and since Abraham had a son he had to marry him off. A numerical reading and a reason for the errand; it does not bear on the English.

apparatus: 24:1.5: the pack's base vowels for the divine name differ from the WLC pointing (יְהֹוָה in the base, יְהוָה in the WLC); the English is the same either way.

segments.english: Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his household, who ruled over all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh, please,
segments.literal: and-said Abraham to his-servant elder-of his-household the-ruling over-all that to-him; put pray your-hand under my-thigh

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: the vav with the imperfect carries the narrative on
adjective 'old' used as a noun; the construct form זְקַן (bound to the next word) is the form Rashi explains
construct chain זְקַן בֵּיתוֹ, 'the elder of his household'
qal participle of מָשַׁל, 'rule'; it qualifies the servant
ב with כֹּל after מָשַׁל: rule 'over' all
לוֹ, 'to him': the relative clause reads 'that is to him', i.e. he had
imperative of שׂוּם
נָא, the particle of entreaty
יָרֵךְ, 'thigh'; the gesture is discussed in the commentary and context

phrases.english: Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his household, who ruled over all that he had,
phrases.literal: and-said Abraham to his-servant elder-of his-household the-ruling over-all that to-him

phrases.english: "Put your hand under my thigh, please,

grammar: The main clause is a wayyiqtol, 'and said'; the speech follows it directly with no second introduction until the servant speaks in 24:5.
שִׂים נָא יָדְךָ תַּחַת יְרֵכִי is an imperative with the particle נָא, 'please'; the object is the hand, and its place is given by תַּחַת.
The servant is described by a construct chain, 'the elder of his household', and one participle with its object, 'who ruled over all that he had'; the English keeps that order.
The gesture itself is the thing to be read: the hand is placed under the thigh of the one who speaks. The meanings given to it are the commentators' and are kept out of the English.
segments.note: The gesture is described plainly. Three readings are recorded: an oath gesture, a sign of being under another's authority, and an allusion to circumcision. Ibn Ezra's choice is not adopted in the English because his explanation is what the gesture meant, which the English does not state.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: some say the gesture alludes to circumcision; he answers that then the man would have sworn by the covenant of circumcision and not by the Name. His own view is that in those days it was the custom for a man to put his hand under the thigh of the one whose authority he was under: 'if you are under my authority, put your hand under my thigh'. The master sits with his thigh over the hand, as in 'here my hand is under your authority, to do your will'. He adds that the custom still exists in the land of Hodu. The English states the gesture only.
Rashi: זקן is pointed as a bound form because it is joined to בית; the vowel is the construct, and the English reads 'the elder of his household'.

Rashi: an oath needs the hand on a holy object, such as a Torah scroll or tefillin; the thigh here is circumcision, the first commandment given to Abraham, which cost him pain and was dear to him. A midrashic-symbolic reading of the gesture; it is recorded, not followed.

Radak: it was a custom that one who charges another puts the hand under his thigh to confirm the matter, as a hand under the thigh is under one's power; it was a strong custom for every agreement, like a covenant between two men.

apparatus: 24:2: the gesture is read three ways in the commentary (oath, subjection, circumcision); the English line gives only 'put your hand under my thigh'.
context: The hand under the thigh (24:2) is a gesture with a plain description: the servant is to put his hand under Abraham's thigh, the thigh of the one who speaks. The same gesture is made by Joseph for Jacob before a promise about Jacob's burial (47:29). The meaning is not stated and is read variously. Ibn Ezra takes it as a sign that the one who places his hand is under the authority of the other, and Radak as a custom for confirming a charge; Rashi takes it as an allusion to circumcision, as the hand rests on something holy. Some also link it to the fact that descendants are said to 'come out of the thigh' (46:26), taking the thigh as the seat of procreation; that is a suggestion, not settled. The text does not choose among these, and the English does not choose.

segments.literal: and-I-will-make-you-swear by-LORD God-of heavens and-God-of earth; that not you-will-take wife for-my-son from-daughters-of the-Canaanite; that I dwell in-its-midst

grammar: The oath is a hifil with a 1st-person subject: 'I will make you swear'. The content of the oath follows in the relative clause אֲשֶׁר לֹא־תִקַּח.
The relative clause is the object of the oath, not a clause about the daughters: 'that you shall not take a wife'.
The epithet is a construct plural, 'God of the heavens and God of the earth'; both parts are kept in the English.
הַכְּנַעֲנִי is singular with the article but collective; the English uses the plural 'Canaanites' for the group.
segments.note: The English keeps the two-part epithet of the oath and the collective Canaanite. The reasons Ibn Ezra gives for the epithet are not part of the English.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra explains the two epithets here: the match of a daughter to a man on earth is made from heaven, and he says this is a secret. It is a reason for the epithets, not a reading of their words.
Ibn Ezra: הַכְּנַעֲנִי is a general term for the eleven nations; the English 'the Canaanites' is the collective.

apparatus: 24:3.2: the pack's base vowels for the divine name differ from the WLC pointing; the English is the same either way.

segments.english: but to my country and to my birthplace you shall go, and take a wife for my son Isaac."
segments.literal: for to my-land and-to my-birthplace you-will-go; and-you-will-take wife for-my-son for-Isaac

tokens.note: כִּי is contrastive after the negative of 24:3: 'but rather'; 'that' is the entry's first sense and is not used here
מוֹלַדְתִּי; the English reads it as the place of birth (see commentary)
qal imperfect 2nd masculine singular of הָלַךְ
waw with a perfect, continuing the command of the imperfect before it
לְיִצְחָק: 'for Isaac', the name in apposition to 'my son'

phrases.english: but to my country and to my birthplace you shall go,
phrases.literal: for to my-land and-to my-birthplace you-will-go

phrases.english: and take a wife for my son Isaac."

grammar: כִּי at the start of the verse turns the negative of 24:3 into a positive command: 'but rather to my country you shall go'.
The two verbs of the command are an imperfect (תֵּלֵךְ) and a perfect with vav (וְלָקַחְתָּ) that continues it.
לִבְנִי לְיִצְחָק gives the son twice, with ל and then the name; the English makes this 'my son Isaac'.
The speech of Abraham that opened in 24:2 closes here.
segments.note: 'Birthplace' takes the place sense of מוֹלֶדֶת that Ibn Ezra, Radak and Rashi give. The kindred sense of the word is in the lexicon entry and is not used in the English.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: 'my land' is Haran, where he lived. The English 'my country' does not name a place.
Ibn Ezra identifies 'my birthplace' (מוֹלַדְתִּי) with Ur of the Chaldeans. The English takes his sense of the word, 'birthplace'; the name of the place is not in the English.
Radak identifies 'my country' with Aram-naharaim, the land of the two rivers. A different identification of the same word; the English does not name the place.

context: 'My country' and 'my birthplace' (24:4, 24:7): Ibn Ezra and Rashi name Haran as the place where Abraham's family settled and Ur of the Chaldeans as the birthplace, though Radak takes 'my country' to be Aram-naharaim. Ramban objects to Ur and takes the two phrases together as the one land of Abraham's kin, where the servant in fact went. The text of this unit names neither place, and the English does not name them.

segments.english: The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman will not be willing to follow me to this land. Shall I indeed bring back your son to the land from which you came?"

the woman who might come (not yet a wife): sense 1

phrases.english: The servant said to him,
"Perhaps the woman will not be willing
to follow me to this land.
Shall I indeed bring back
your son to the land
from which you came?"

grammar: The servant's speech is two questions: a doubt, 'perhaps the woman will not be willing', and a question, 'shall I bring your son back?'
הֶהָשֵׁב אָשִׁיב is an infinitive absolute before a finite form of the same root: an emphatic question that the English states once.
The same noun, 'the land', is used twice: once with the demonstrative 'this', once with a relative clause 'from which you came'.
The servant speaks of Abraham's son by the suffix 'your son', and of the woman as the object of 'follow me'.
segments.note: The English gives 'shall I indeed bring back' for the emphatic question: 'indeed' carries the infinitive absolute. Ibn Ezra's comment on the pointing of the he is not a reading of the words and is kept in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: אוּלַי has many senses and he cites another occurrence of the word. The English takes 'perhaps', the first sense in the entry.

Ibn Ezra explains the short patah under the he of הֶהָשֵׁב: a long patah would be heavy on the tongue, because the he of the hifil carries a qamets. A note on the pointing; the English does not depend on it.
Sforno reads the relative clause 'from which you came' as implying that you have despised that place, so the woman will not want to come here. The English keeps the plain relative clause.

segments.english: Abraham said to him, "Take heed to yourself, lest you bring back my son there.
segments.literal: and-said to-him Abraham; take-heed to-you; lest you-will-bring-back; ACC; my-son there

tokens.note: nifal imperative of שָׁמַר, 'be on your guard'
ל with the suffix: the reflexive 'to yourself'
פֶּן with the imperfect: the feared result
hifil imperfect 2nd masculine singular of שׁוּב, the servant as subject
object marker: no English

phrases.english: Abraham said to him,
"Take heed to yourself,
lest you bring back
my son there.

grammar: הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ is a nifal imperative with a dative suffix: 'take heed to yourself'.
פֶּן with the imperfect gives the result Abraham fears: 'lest you bring back my son there'.
Abraham's answer is one speech that opens here and runs to the end of 24:8.
segments.note: The English keeps the servant as 'you' throughout. The root is שׁמר, 'keep'; the nifal sense 'be on your guard' is the one the warning requires. Ibn Ezra's rule on the stress of הִשָּׁמֶר puts this form, stressed on the penult, under שְׁמִירָה, so it agrees with the English.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: every הִשָּׁמֶר stressed on the penultimate syllable comes from שְׁמִירָה (keeping); one stressed on the last comes from שְׁמָרִים (lees, dregs), as in 'be still and quiet' (Isaiah 7:4), like 'he is at ease on his lees' (Jeremiah 48:11). The form here has its accent on the shin, the penultimate syllable, so by his own rule it is from שׁמר 'keep', and the English 'take heed' agrees.
Radak: Abraham did not want the son to leave the land that God gave him and his seed. A reason for the warning; not a reading of the words.

phrases.english: The LORD, God of heaven,
who took me from my father's house and from the land of my birth,
phrases.literal: who took-me from-house-of my-father and-from-land-of my-birth

phrases.english: and who spoke to me
and who swore to me,
saying, 'To your offspring I will give
this land';
may he send his angel before you,
and you shall take a wife for my son from there.

grammar: Three relative clauses, each with אֲשֶׁר, hang from 'the LORD, God of heaven': who took me, who spoke to me, who swore to me. The main clause begins with 'he will send'.
לֵאמֹר לְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן אֶת־הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת is speech inside Abraham's speech, so it is in single quotes.
The yiqtol הוּא יִשְׁלַח is read as a wish, 'may he send'; the next verse's 'if the woman will not be willing' supports Ibn Ezra's reading (see commentary).
The weqatal וְלָקַחְתָּ continues the purpose of the sending: 'and you shall take a wife'.
segments.note: The epithet 'God of heaven' stands alone here, unlike 24:3, where 'and God of earth' is added. Rashi explains the difference; the English keeps the words as they stand. The yiqtol הוּא יִשְׁלַח can be read as a plain future, 'he will send his angel', or as a wish, 'may he send his angel'. The English takes the wish with Ibn Ezra (a prayer, since the woman may refuse in 24:8) and Sforno; the plain future is the other reading and is recorded in the context.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: 'he will send his angel' is a prayer, not a prophecy; if it were prophecy he would not go on to say 'if the woman will not be willing' (24:8). The English reads the yiqtol as a wish, 'may he send'; the plain future is the other reading and is recorded in the note and the context.
Sforno reads the clause as a wish: may he send his angel from his holy dwelling in the heavens, since he took me from there, so that my son need not go there. This supports the wish reading.

Rashi explains why the epithet here is 'God of heaven' alone: when God took Abraham from his father's house he was 'God of heaven and not God of earth', because the people of the world did not know him and his name was not common in the land. A reason for the wording, not a reading of its grammar.
Rashi: 'my father's house' is Haran. The English keeps 'my father's house'.
Rashi: 'the land of my birth' is Ur of the Chaldeans. The English keeps 'the land of my birth'.
Rashi: לִי here means 'for my sake', 'about me' (like עָלַי), as with verbs of speaking; the English 'spoke to me' keeps the plain preposition.

apparatus: 24:7.1: the epithet is 'God of heaven' without 'and God of earth' as in 24:3; the commentators' explanations are in the commentary.
context: 'My father's house' and 'the land of my birth' (24:7): Rashi names Haran and Ur of the Chaldeans; the text of this unit names neither.

'May he send his angel' (24:7): the verb is a yiqtol, which allows a plain future ('he will send his angel') or a wish. Ibn Ezra takes it as a prayer, because Abraham goes on to allow that the woman may be unwilling (24:8); Sforno also reads a wish. The plain future is the other reading; Abraham uses the same words when he tells the servant's story in 24:40.

אַחֲרֶיךָ

phrases.english: If the woman will not be willing to follow you,
phrases.literal: and-if not she-will-be-willing the-woman to-go after-you

phrases.english: then you shall be clear of this oath of mine;
only my son
you shall not bring back there."

grammar: The conditional has a protasis (8.1 to 8.6), 'if the woman will not be willing', and an apodosis (8.7) introduced by the vav of נִקִּיתָ: 'then you shall be clear'.
נִקִּיתָ is a nifal perfect of a III-he verb: the pattern is regular, and the English 'shall be clear' gives the nifal sense of freedom from an obligation.
The last clause puts the object first: רַק אֶת־בְּנִי לֹא תָשֵׁב שָׁמָּה, 'only my son you shall not bring back there'. The restriction applies to the son alone.
The speech closes here, at the end of the unit's last verse.
segments.note: The English gives the plain sense of the hifil: the servant is not to bring the son back. Ibn Ezra's remark (that Isaac is to stay in the land of Israel, for Abraham's sake) states what the prohibition secures and is recorded in the commentary. Rashi's reading of the release (a wife from the daughters of Aner, Eshkol and Mamre) is recorded and not followed.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: 'you shall not bring him back there' means that Isaac is to stay in the land of Israel; the reason for 'you shall not bring back' is Abraham, who is the principal. The English keeps the hifil with the servant as subject and Isaac as object.
Rashi reads the release from the oath as permission to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of Aner, Eshkol and Mamre. The Hebrew here names no family; the English keeps 'be clear of this oath'.
Rashi: רַק is a limit, 'my son does not return', and Jacob his grandson will in the end return. A later reading; the English 'only' is the same word.

context: Aner, Eshkol and Mamre (24:8, Rashi) are named in chapter 14 as Abraham's allies; the text of this unit does not name them as the family for Isaac's wife.
